t:
(a) Victims’ Rights.—
        (1) In general.—Subchapter I of chapter 47 of title 10, United States Code (the Uniform Code of Military Justice), is amended by adding at the end the following new section (article):“§ 806b. Art. 6b. Rights of the victim of an offense under this chapter“(a) Rights of a Victim of an Offense Under This Chapter.—A victim of an offense under this chapter has the following rights:“(1) The right to be reasonably protected from the accused.“(2) The right to reasonable, accurate, and timely notice of any of the following:“(A) A public hearing concerning the continuation of confinement prior to trial of the accused.“(B) A preliminary hearing under section 832 of this title (article 32) relating to the offense.“(C) A court-martial relating to the offense.“(D) A public proceeding of the service clemency and parole board relating to the offense.“(E) The release or escape of the accused, unless such notice may endanger the safety of any person.“(3) The right not to be excluded from any public hearing or proceeding described in paragraph (2) unless the military judge or investigating officer, as applicable, after receiving clear and convincing evidence, determines that testimony by the victim of an offense under this chapter would be materially altered if the victim heard other testimony at that hearing or proceeding.“(4) The right to be reasonably heard at any of the following:“(A) A public hearing concerning the continuation of confinement prior to trial of the accused.“(B) A sentencing hearing relating to the offense.“(C) A public proceeding of the service clemency and parole board relating to the offense.“(5) The reasonable right to confer with the counsel representing the Government at any proceeding described in paragraph (2).“(6) The right to receive restitution as provided in law.“(7) The right to proceedings free from unreasonable delay.“(8) The right to be treated with fairness and with respect for the dignity and privacy of the victim of an offense under this chapter.“(b) Victim of an Offense Under This Chapter Defined.—In this section, the term ‘victim of an offense under this chapter’ means a person who has suffered direct physical, emotional, or pecuniary harm as a result of the commission of an offense under this chapter (the Uniform Code of Military Justice).“(c) Legal Guardian for Certain Victims.—In the case of a victim of an offense under this chapter who is under 18 years of age, incompetent, incapacitated, or deceased, the military judge shall designate a legal guardian from among the representatives of the estate of the victim, a family member, or other suitable person to assume the victim’s rights under this section. However, in no event may the person so designated be the accused.“(d) Rule of Construction.—Nothing in this section (article) shall be construed—“(1) to authorize a cause of action for damages; or“(2) to create, to enlarge, or to imply any duty or obligation to any victim of an offense under this chapter or other person for the breach of which the United States or any of its officers or employees could be held liable in damages.”
. 
        (2) Clerical amendment.—The table of sections at the beginning of subchapter I of chapter 47 of such title (the Uniform Code of Military Justice) is amended by adding at the end the following new item:

“806b. 
Art. 6b. Rights of the victim of an offense under this chapter.”.

  
    (b) Implementation.—
        (1) Issuance.—Not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act—
            (A) the Secretary of Defense shall recommend to the President changes to the Manual for Courts-Martial to implement section 806b of title 10, United States Code (article 6b of the Uniform Code of Military Justice), as added by subsection (a); and 
            (B) the Secretary of Defense and Secretary of Homeland Security (with respect to the Coast Guard when it is not operating as a service in the Navy) shall prescribe such regulations as each such Secretary considers appropriate to implement such section.  
        (2) Mechanisms for affording rights.—The recommendations and regulations required by paragraph (1) shall include the following:
            (A) Mechanisms for ensuring that victims are notified of, and accorded, the rights specified in section 806b of title 10, United States Code (article 6b of the Uniform Code of Military Justice), as added by subsection (a). 
            (B) Mechanisms for ensuring that members of the Armed Forces and civilian personnel of the Department of Defense and the Coast Guard make their best efforts to ensure that victims are notified of, and accorded, the rights specified in such section. 
            (C) Mechanisms for the enforcement of such rights, including mechanisms for application for such rights and for consideration and disposition of applications for such rights. 
            (D) The designation of an authority within each Armed Force to receive and investigate complaints relating to the provision or violation of such rights. 
            (E) Disciplinary sanctions for members of the Armed Forces and other personnel of the Department of Defense and Coast Guard who willfully or wantonly fail to comply with requirements relating to such rights.

fable.w: The section directs the Secretaries to prescribe regulations implementing the victims' rights article, and a statutory requirement to issue regulations counts as participation under the definition. It also gives victims, who are outside the government, a right to be reasonably heard at confinement hearings and clemency and parole board proceedings. The tempting reading is that this is only individual-case adjudication within the military justice system, with a rule of construction denying a damages action, but the rulemaking mandate is enough on its own to cross the federal boundary.
fable.s: the Secretary of Defense and Secretary of Homeland Security (with respect to the Coast Guard when it is not operating as a service in the Navy) shall prescribe such regulations as each such Secretary considers appropriate to implement such section.

qwen_block.w: The section grants victims of military offenses, who are outside the federal government, the right to be heard at public hearings and proceedings. This constitutes participation because it allows non-federal individuals to directly influence or provide input during federal decision-making processes (such as sentencing or parole). The definition explicitly includes public hearings and the ability to be heard as forms of participation.
qwen_block.s: (4) The right to be reasonably heard at any of the following: (A) A public hearing concerning the continuation of confinement prior to trial of the accused. (B) A sentencing hearing relating to the offense. (C) A public proceeding of the service clemency and parole board relating to the offense.

opus.w: The section requires federal agencies to issue regulations, and the definition counts required rulemaking as participation. It also gives crime victims, who are outside the government, the 'right to be reasonably heard' at public hearings before federal decisions on pretrial confinement, sentencing, and clemency or parole. A 'No' reading would rest on two points: the recommendations to the President stay inside the government, and the victim hearings concern single cases. Neither point outweighs the separate requirement to issue regulations.
opus.s: the Secretary of Defense and Secretary of Homeland Security (with respect to the Coast Guard when it is not operating as a service in the Navy) shall prescribe such regulations as each such Secretary considers appropriate to implement such section.
opus.b: Someone might read this section as "No" for two reasons. First, a victim's right to be heard in a court-martial or parole case concerns one person's case, much like the manufacturer's chance to respond in Example 11, rather than a policy decision. Second, the Secretaries are required to send changes to the Manual for Courts-Martial to the President, which is a step that stays inside the federal government. Neither point settles it. Subsection (b)(1)(B) separately requires the Secretaries to issue regulations, and under the definition (and Example 6), requiring rulemaking counts as "Yes." On top of that, victims, who are outside the government, get a right to be heard at public hearings before federal decisions on pretrial confinement, sentencing, and clemency or parole.

qwen_chat.w: This section grants procedural rights to victims within the military justice system, such as the right to be heard at hearings. However, it explicitly disclaims any right to sue the government for damages or breach of duty. The definition of participation requires the government to consult or coordinate with outsiders before making a decision, or grants the right to sue. Military justice proceedings are adjudicative, not consultative, and the victims are parties to the case, not external advisors or participants in a policy-making process. The explicit exclusion of a cause of action further distinguishes this from the 'right to sue' criterion for participation.
qwen_chat.s: Nothing in this section (article) shall be construed—(1) to authorize a cause of action for damages; or (2) to create, to enlarge, or to imply any duty or obligation to any victim of an offense under this chapter or other person for the breach of which the United States or any of its officers or employees could be held liable in damages.
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that granting victims the right to be heard at hearings or to confer with counsel constitutes "participation" because it involves non-federal individuals interacting with the government during a decision-making process (the military justice process). However, the definition explicitly states that participation involves consulting or coordinating with people outside the government *before* making a decision, often in an advisory or rulemaking context. More importantly, the definition excludes "applications for benefits" and focuses on the *government's* obligation to consult outsiders. While victims have rights here, this is a procedural right within a judicial/quasi-judicial process (military justice), not a mechanism for the government to seek input from the public or outside entities to inform a policy or administrative decision. The "participation" definition is typically reserved for advisory committees, public comment periods, or consultations with states/tribes/experts on policy. Military justice proceedings are internal government functions (even if involving civilians as victims/accused), and the rights granted are due process rights, not "participation" in the sense of the definition (which emphasizes the government seeking input from outsiders). Furthermore, the victims are often service members (inside the government) or civilians, but the process is adjudicative, not advisory/policy-making. The definition's examples (advisory boards, comment periods, consultation with states) do not fit this scenario. The key is that the government is not *consulting* the victim to *make* a decision; the victim is a party to a proceeding.

However, let's look closer at the definition: "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." And "It does include the ability to sue the government over a decision." It does *not* explicitly include being a party to a trial. The victims here are parties to a military justice proceeding. Is a military justice proceeding a "federal decision" in the sense of the definition? The definition focuses on "consult or coordinate... before making a decision". In a trial, the victim doesn't "consult" the judge; they present evidence. This is adversarial, not consultative. Therefore, it is likely "No".

Let's re-read the "No" traps: "applications for benefits...". This isn't an application. "reports to Congress...". No. "consultation... between federal agencies". No.

Let's re-read the "Yes" criteria: "requiring a public comment period... public hearing... advisory committee... consultation with states... right to sue".

Does the victim have a "right to sue"? No, subsection (d)(1) explicitly says "Nothing in this section... shall be construed to authorize a cause of action for damages".

Is there a "public hearing" where the public participates? The victim has a right to be present and heard. But is this "participation" as defined? The definition says "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." The victim is not being consulted; they are a party. The government (prosecution) is representing the government. The victim is an individual. This is a legal right, not a participatory process in the administrative/policy sense.

Therefore, the label is "No".
